extracted.intended_audience: aspiring writers and young literati considering a literary career
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and moral guidance for young people who feel disposed to become authors, covering career choices, work habits, principles of journalism and political writing, and methods of reading and historical inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never pursue literature as a trade
rubrics_metrics.description: Never pursue literature as a trade; do not make authorship your sole business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With the exception of one extraordinary man, the writer advises against depending on the sale of works for a living. Money and immediate reputation 'form only an arbitrary and accidental end of literary labour' and when necessity drives writing it converts the stimulant of hope into a narcotic that 'stun[s] and stupif[ies] the mind.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Hold some regular employment or profession
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep some regular employment (a profession or trade) alongside literary work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A steady occupation provides three hours of leisure 'unannoyed by any alien anxiety' that will allow more genial literary output than weeks of compulsion. Regular employment supplies sympathy with the world, a quicker tact for common subjects, keeps one from being considered merely an author, and increases chances of domestic happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide talents and genius between profession and literary pursuits
rubrics_metrics.description: Devote talents to acquiring competence in a known trade or profession and reserve genius for tranquil and unbiassed literary choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author counsels a practical division: use talents to secure competence/competence in a profession; use genius for literary objects chosen freely. The conscious desire to perform duty ennobles both pursuits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer leisure writing over compelled production
rubrics_metrics.description: Work on literature in leisure time that is looked forward to, not as a forced task.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three hours of peaceful leisure are presented as sufficient to produce more genuinely genial writing than prolonged, pressured work. The presence of family or the atmosphere of home should not be treated as interruptions but as restorative to writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making monetary or reputational gain the dominant motive
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not let the necessity of acquiring money or immediate reputation drive your literary labour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns that excessive motive reverses nature of inspiration; hopes of pay or fame may act as stimulants but can become destructive when they become necessities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scrutinize your motives for indolence, restlessness, or vanity
rubrics_metrics.description: Strictly examine whether scruples against a profession or course are genuine or masks for indolence, restlessness, or impatient vanity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The youthful objector should catalogue scruples, ensure they arise from conscientious reflection, have read foundational works on the subject, and seek examples of others who resolved similar doubts responsibly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay irrevocable literary commitments until mature judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Postpone permanent or early exclusive commitments to authorship until manhood and further experience have advanced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time spent delaying is 'time won'—manhood brings knowledge, judgment, and temperance of feeling. Even if delay doesn't change the decision, it prevents rashness and vanity from tainting a final choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine literature with domestic and social life
rubrics_metrics.description: Be something besides an author; combine literary work with an active domestic and social life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being engaged in other occupations makes an author more accessible socially, prevents silence being seen as pride, and improves genuine admiration because accomplishments surpass expectations. Domestic life offers superior chance of happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: The established Church (or comparable institution) can aid literary development
rubrics_metrics.description: An established church or similar profession provides a favourable environment and patronage for scholars and men of genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The clergyman is portrayed as neighbour and family-man, able to visit different social strata and to foster learning; church revenues circulate as reversionary property and support education—this is advanced as an effective and unburdensome patronage for learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious of the trade-like degeneration of authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid becoming a mere 'servant of the press' or 'book-letter setter' by indiscriminate, frequent publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting Herder: excessive or premature use of authorship makes 'the head waste and the heart empty'; sending every passing thought to print depletes a writer and reduces them to a mere servant of the printing trade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic impartiality and declared principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct journals and essays on fixed, announced principles and adhere honestly to them; practise genuine impartiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impartiality is defined as 'an honest and enlightened adherence to a code of intelligible principles previously announced' and to refer to them in support of judgments—not indiscriminate abuse, not indulging an editor's malignant passions, nor pandering to vulgar appetites for profit. The author credits such practice with securing newspaper success without party patronage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pandering or flattery to gain sales
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not write to flatter envy, cupidity, vindictiveness, or the half-witted vulgar for money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author condemns the determination 'to make money by flattering' base popular sentiments as almost fiendish and a corrupting motive for editors and writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place current events in a moral point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: In political and journalistic writing, place questions and events of the day in a moral perspective, tracing particular measures to permanent principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Essays should give dignity to measures by tracing policy or impolicy to enduring principles, and give interest to principles by applying them to individual measures. This method improves public understanding and moral framing of events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use historical comparison and primary sources in political writing
rubrics_metrics.description: When analyzing political events, seek contemporary historians and original documents, compare with past similar events, subtract differences, and judge by the balance of likenesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author describes procuring 'original documents of the past' and 'authentic accounts of the present,' then fairly subtracting points of difference from likeness; where the balance favours likeness, conjecture that the result will be similar. He cites examples like comparing France under Napoleon with Rome under the Caesars and the United Provinces with Spain under Philip II.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define and analyze political terms precisely
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly define and analyze political terms rather than letting them be mere terms of abuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the author claims to have 'first explicitly defined and analyzed the nature of Jacobinism,' distinguishing it from republican, democrat, and the mere demagogue, thereby rescuing the word from becoming merely abusive and alerting honest minds to genuine dangers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read to discern a writer's ignorance before assuming their understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: When reading philosophical or other works, adopt the maxim: 'until you understand a writer's ignorance, presume yourself ignorant of his understanding.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply received and ascertained laws to explain strange incidents in fanatic writers without assuming intentional falsehood; use the maxim as a method to detect the limits of a writer's insight and to approach texts with humility and critical attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value non-published forms of intellectual influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure a scholar's utility not solely by published books but by the truths and minds he helps to circulate and stimulate by conversation and correspondence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that influence through lectures, conversations, letters, and the excitation of other minds may be as or more valuable than the mere number of publications; reprints and republication of essays in other journals can also indicate usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware rhetorical and stylistic excesses that reduce clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid disproportionate demands on attention: excess refinement, over-elaboration, length and laborious sentence construction, obscurity, and a love of paradox.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The writer acknowledges that his prose has been criticized for these faults and concedes that these are defects to be mindful of. The counsel is implicit: strive for clarity and avoid needlessly elaborate style that hampers comprehension.
